displayQuote: Be soft. Do not let the world make you hard. Do not let the pain make you hate. Do not let the bitterness steal your sweetness

meta.title: Who really said "Be soft. Do not let the world make you hard"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Kurt Vonnegut. It is a 2007 blog poem called 'The Fur' by Iain S. Thomas, later collected in 'I Wrote This For You'. Thomas is alive, has said so repeatedly, and owns the copyright.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Be soft. Do not let the world make you hard'?
meta.ogDescription: Iain S. Thomas wrote it on a blog in 2007. The Vonnegut credit is an invention — and the Vonnegut Museum and the Vonnegut Society both say so.

answer.label: Verified — and the author is alive to say so
answer.authorDates: b. 1980 · South African poet, writing as ‘pleasefindthis’
answer.sourceLine: It is a prose poem titled The Fur, posted in August 2007 on the blog I Wrote This For You under the pen name pleasefindthis, and later collected in the book of the same name. The author, Iain S. Thomas, is alive, has written a first-person account of the misattribution, and still spends his time asking strangers to stop selling his poem with Kurt Vonnegut’s name on it.

source.excerpt: Be soft. Do not let the world make you hard. Do not let the pain make you hate. Do not let the bitterness steal your sweetness.
trail: The poem exists at a fixed address with a date on it: The Fur, posted to the I Wrote This For You blog in August 2007, years before the line began circulating with a novelist’s name attached the original post ↗.

Thomas wrote his own account of what happened for HuffPost in April 2016 — he reproduces the poem, explains he published it anonymously, and describes someone deciding it ‘needed to have been said by someone more important… than some, still living, semi-anonymous blogger’ his account ↗.

We did not stop at the author’s word. The Vonnegut end was checked independently: the Kurt Vonnegut Museum and Library and a vice-president of the Kurt Vonnegut Society both confirmed to fact-checkers that the passage appears nowhere in his work the fact-check ↗.
source.excerptNote: Quoted here for identification and commentary. The poem carries on for one more sentence after this — the part almost nobody reposts — about still believing the world to be a beautiful place.

sourceLink.text: Iain S. Thomas on having his poem taken

source.rightsNote: In copyright, and the point of the page. Iain S. Thomas is a working poet, alive, and this is his text — protected for his lifetime plus seventy years. He gives the poems away free online in the hope that someone buys a book, which is exactly the model the Vonnegut credit destroys: a dead novelist’s name makes the poem feel like heritage, free for a mug, a candle or a wall print. It is not. Quote it briefly with his name on it; do not sell it. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Iain S. Thomas
author.heading: About Iain S. Thomas
author.metaLine: b. 1980 · South African poet, author of I Wrote This For You
author.bio: Iain S. Thomas began posting short prose poems in 2007 under the name pleasefindthis, pairing them with photographs by Jon Ellis. The project became I Wrote This For You, a book in 2011 and a poetry bestseller since. He is the unusual case of an author who watched a single piece of his own writing become globally famous under someone else’s name, and who has spent years politely, publicly and repeatedly correcting it — a living rebuttal you can email.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: Most quote mysteries end with a shrug. This one ends with a phone number: the author is alive, he has said in print that he wrote it, and the estate-adjacent bodies for the man he is confused with have independently agreed.

items.why: The passage appears in no Vonnegut novel, essay, letter or speech. The Kurt Vonnegut Museum and Library and an officer of the Kurt Vonnegut Society have both said so on the record. Vonnegut died in April 2007 — months before the poem was posted the check ↗.

Vonnegut really did write plain, kind, aphoristic advice — ‘God damn it, you’ve got to be kind’ is genuinely his. The poem sounds close enough to pass a two-second sniff test, which is all most reposts get.
Thomas published under a pen name with no byline attached to the image versions. A poem with no author is a vacancy, and the internet fills vacancies with famous dead men.
It has run in newspapers as ‘the words made famous by American author Kurt Vonnegut’, and been used to sell other people’s books — which is what finally made a quiet poet start replying in public.

The line still turns up on quote forums under Vonnegut’s name, and Thomas still turns up underneath to say it is his. Treat any such account as a claim, not proof — but here the claim matches a dated 2007 post, a signed magazine essay and two independent Vonnegut authorities.

misattribution.truthLine: Iain S. Thomas, The Fur, August 2007 — a living author, a dated post, and a book you can buy his own account ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It gives permission. Almost every other piece of advice about a hard world tells you to toughen up; this one says the toughening is the injury, and that staying sweet is the achievement. That is why it ends up in cards, eulogies and tattoos.

It also has the shape of something old — short imperative sentences, no proper nouns, no slang to date it. Nothing in the text tells you it was typed on a blog in 2007, which is precisely how it slipped into the public domain in people’s heads.
context.detailsSummary: What the wrong name actually costs
detailsBody: Attribution is not vanity for a poet who gives work away free online. The free poem is the advertisement; the book is the income. Strip the name and the model collapses.
A dead-author credit does something worse than misinform: it makes a protected text look like heritage, and heritage looks free to print on a candle.
Thomas has said the corrections rarely stick — the misattributed image outruns the reply every time, because the wrong version is the one with the famous name on it.
This site’s usual finding is that getting the attribution right frees a text. Here it does the reverse, and that is the honest result.
context.pull: Vonnegut died in April 2007. The poem was posted that August.
